newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - WH Smith doubles profits in 1st half.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - WH Smith doubles profits in 1st half.

text.p: Britain's biggest bookseller W.H. Smith Group Plc produced a thumping increase in first half profits on Wednesday, but said improving sales and earnings at its core chain of stores would be a long haul.

The retailer, also owner of specialist book stores Waterstones, and the Virgin/Our Price music shops, more than doubled pretax profits in the first half to 38.6 million pounds ($62.3 million) from 17.3 million.
Sales from ongoing businesses rose by two percent to 1.29 billion pounds. December sales were up six percent overall and ahead three percent on a like-for-like basis.
The group, which made the first loss in its 204 year history last year, embarked on a four year revival plan last June.
Chief executive Bill Cockburn said the reorganisation, including the sale of Niceday office supplies and Do It All home improvement stores, had created a springboard for growing top line profits.
The results beat market forecasts and Smiths' shares stood 8.5 pence higher at 438.5 pence.
Cockburn told Reuters in an interview the main W.H. Smith retail chain was now the top priority for action.
"It's very important that we get that fixed and that's going to be a long haul, but we'll have benefits along the way."
Cockburn, who took the helm just a year ago, said new management had to capitalise on the strengths of Smiths' well-loved brand name.
He said 7.5 million shoppers visited the shops every week, but the key was to persuade them to spend and persuade those who did spend to spend more.

Smith's "High Street" stores have suffered from the huge expansion of out-of-town superstores. Competition has hotted up as food retailers muscled in on Smith's traditional market by selling books, videos, stationery and greeting cards.
Cockburn said Smiths held on to the top slots in market share in books, video, music, magazines, stationery and childrens "back to school" equipment.
"Of course competition is building up, but we're holding our market shares in the key areas pretty well."

Management had been vigorous in ridding the stores of unprofitable "clutter" and freeing up space for more profitable use. Smiths will extend its new childrens' discovery range, trialled in 12 stores, into its larger shops. The group also plans to sell CDs and tapes in 90 of its smaller stores after a successful trial.
Cost cutting delivered savings of nine million pounds in the first half, with 14 million expected for the full year.

Cockburn said boosting sales growth in the core chain was a top priority, but did not want to buy' sales by diluting gross margin. "I don't think there's any mileage in buying sales by just discounting to uneconomic levels," he said.

Cockburn said sales, including Christmas and into the new year, had been encouraging considering the upheaval caused by the reorganisation. Sales since December had continued at the same sort of level.

Profits at Waterstones rose to 9.1 million pounds from 7.4 million and like-for-like sales were up nine percent. But a lackluster music scene hit Virgin/Our Price, which lost 1.4 million pounds and saw sales fall two percent to 194 million.
W.H. Smith held its dividend at 5.25 pence, but said it expected to introduce a progressive dividend policy as its financial performance improved.

When asked about recent speculation in the press about a bid for W.H. Smith, Cockburn said, "We are the biggest seller of fiction in the country and sometimes we read fiction in the newspapers as well."
